fullContext:
Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Hey, everyone, and welcome back to the Information, uh, Bottleneck Podcast. And today we have Zhuang Liu. He's a assistant professor, uh, at Princeton. Hi, Zhuang. Nice to have you.

Zhuang Liu: Hi, Ravid. Mm. Hi, Alan. Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And as always, we have Alan. Hey, Alan.

Allen Roush: It's good to see you again, Ravid. Nice to meet you, Zhuang. And, uh, yeah, you should go take a look at his Google Scholar. He has a lot of really cool papers.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Yeah, so we'll talk about some of these papers, uh, today. And in general, we are going to talk about what are the important components, uh, in today AIs. Okay? So you have so, Zhuang, you have so many works. Uh, I think we can start with some understanding of what do you think are the important component. So, uh, a few years ago, you had a paper about, uh, a conv, a convnet for the 2020s, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Um, that, you know what? Maybe you'll tell us about what is the, the paper about, and then we can start to, to start to decompose the-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... the components for current, uh, AI systems.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Yes, of course. So that was a really interesting story. So the paper, we, we were working on this paper in twen- 2021, and back then, transformers has just entered the computer vision's, world, computer vision research space, through the introduction of vision transformers, right? And then everybody from the vision community have, have been, switching to vision transformers from more traditional convnets, and they are getting better and better performance. So in, so in this work, we want to say, we want to investigate, whether truly, like, convnet is, has lost its, competitiveness, and whether it's possible to, to, control all the design components there is to study whether convnets can be modernized to be, on par with vision transformers at that time.

So we wanna study whether it's a, it's a difference that seeming, seemingly, performance gap between transform- vision transformers and convnets is due to their inherent design, like whether you use self-attention or convolution or due to other small, like seemingly small design details. So, and we found the answer to be, the latter. So after a lot of studying, in, of like modernizing the design compon- components of a convnet, we eventually get the model to be on par with, vision transformers, very strong vision transformers at that time on a diverse range of tasks. So this demonstrates that, no matter you choose convnet or vision transformers, as long as you get the des- the, everything correct, you'll, you'll get, the same frontier level performance on vision tasks.

Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And do you still believe that this is true? Do you still believe that like at the end, it doesn't really matter?

Zhuang Liu: I wouldn't s-- Yeah, I, I largely tend to agree, but I wou- I wouldn't say it doesn't matter. it's, I, I would say, as long as you get everything correct, like as long as you have, y- explore the s- the design space enough, you'll converge to some point where it's like kind of the Pareto frontier in terms of accuracy and efficiency trade-off. And it's very hard to go off this frontier. like I think in the past, many years, there haven't been real- really, like innovations that, have been widely adopted other than the, kind of the mature architectures that we, we already were working with, several years ago. but, but this process itself is very, very fun. in fact, recently there have been some, paper releases on this, especially from this, open, open weight model companies like Kimi, DeepSeek.

They're still playing around with architectures, like how do you, how do you change residual connections? How do you, connect different layers? these kind of stuff. And, and I respect that work a lot. In fact, part of the reason that architecture research is less active in academia right now is that, we couldn't really afford to, afford the compute to demonstrate these effects in, in, convincing scale. So that's a, a sad part, but I still try to play around with it myself using our, resources at, at, university. actually, with the help of Cloud Code, I can now, go back to coding to, to play around in the first hand myself. So this is very fun research, but in, I do think in, from a practical stand, point of view, what data we learn, what data we train the model on matters more than, the architecture choice.

As long as the interface, the input/output interface stays the same, architecture, architecture is how we parameterize the function approximator, right? The, the very basic function of, of neural networks or deep learning. And how we parameterize it, no matter, as long as you get like a few things correct, like using residual connections, using self-attention or, or other like, reasonable mechanisms, and having the right activation at the right places, feed forward, layers at the right places, you'll be at the f- very close or at the frontier, curve of this, performance, versus efficiency, balance. And, then I was, I, I would tend to think that what, what matters more in terms of practical usage, in terms of bringing the product to more and more people to be more effective in their daily usage.

I do think other, other aspects like what data has this model been trained on, how it can handle context and memory is what, what matters more. So in terms of context and memory, yes, there are-- there do exist architectural work that, address that. So I think that is kind of the more immediate problems we, we need to address in, in making AI like up another level. Yeah.

Allen Roush: In a ConvNet for the 2020s, uh, first of all, you know, maybe just give your summary of that paper, but, but then my, my question is, um, you know, as I read it, uh, it looks like you, you gr-- and also correct me if this, uh, uh, my understanding is wrong, but my understanding is you gradually modernize ResNet towards a Swin-like design and end up-

Zhuang Liu: Right

Allen Roush: ... with a ConvNet that competes strongly with transformers. Um, which single ablation did you, like in that paper, most changed your own mind about where the supposed transformer advantage was really coming from?

Zhuang Liu: what ablation? I think it's every ablation. If you, if you look at the graph, nothing single-handedly, transformed, like brought, brought up the performance by large margin. Like some of them are more useful than others, but, it's not really that one change changed everything. maybe the, I, I guess the use of activation and norm-- redu-reduction of normalization layers is one thing that, kind of intrigued me and, has a noticeable performance change. but it was really everything together. So these seemingly small components, when we compound them together, they can, they can really cause large differences that would normally attribute to, some, some substantial change, like changing convolution to a self-attention or in, into, modernized, say, more modern mechanisms like linear attention, right?

So, so I think the, the big lesson here is, these small details when combined together matters much more than the sim- seemingly core components of the networks. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: But do you think it's-- because for me, it looks that like we have, like we are trying a lot of things. Some of these things are working, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And then we get better models.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And then like in retrospective, like we can, we can start like to understand like exactly what the component that are actually matter, right? Like we can-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... try to, oh, so now let's change ConvNet and, and make it look, looks more as a, as a transformer, for example, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Um, do you agree with that? Do you think that like this is something that we actually need, need this breakthrough, and then we can trace back and, uh, understand the, the details and try to match other methods? Or do you think like we just need to try again and again, and, uh, we don't need the very specific, uh, directions?

Zhuang Liu: I see. Got it. Yeah, I think transformer absolutely is a blessing to the, to the community and also the vision transformers, the, the adoption of transformers in computer vision. I don't debate that. That's, that's hard to debate. it's, it's absolutely a breakthrough, a very important breakthrough. perh- perhaps the, the biggest breakthrough in, in that, years. and, so our study was more focusing on like computer vision only domains. But another benefit of vision transformers is that they, they allow the unification of, of text and image representations, right? it's, it's then the use of transformer is very important for later developments like, LLaVA, like this multimodal framework where you have text enc-- vision encoders encode the vision into tokens, and then just treat tokens, get them together to be fed into a, a downstream LLMs.

It's a basic framework of a lot of multimodal models right now. So I think, the adoption of transformers in vision is v- a big stamp, big step for unification of multimodal data. This is, back to the, our study. Investigation of details, I, I would say it's more of a lesson. It's l- not, I think it changed my understanding more than, more than like... I'm, I'm more proud of this work because it changes my own understanding and some other, a lot of other people's understanding rather than like we now can go really, like you can still stay with ConvNets. I, I-- people can still do that. The ConvNets has its own benefits as well, especially when, restricted to computer vision only.

It's, it's convenient to deploy. It's, kind of easier to understand, especially it, may also have, better support for higher resolution long con-- long, long sequences because the operation is local. I, I, I think they just excel at different places. and this, this study-... transformation of details is a, a, is more kind of a lesson for me rather than like, we need to figure out each component, how, how much they contributes to, to performance, difference. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: So, okay. So these are, uh, okay, so, so architecture is not so important, and you also like you have a more recent paper that you actually showed that, uh, uh, normalization layers are not so important, right? That you can basically can, um, remove normalization layer using, uh, um, uh, a tangent, uh, um, activation function, right? And, and maybe you need to do, uh, some tweak and, and to, to, to treat it a bit differently, but-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... it works fine.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: So what do you think is the, what do you think are the important components and, you know, the core components that you say like, okay, these are so important for AI, for deep learning, and, and why Only in the recent years, like we, we came up with such good models. Well, why-- if, if architecture, um, doesn't matter, why we only have good AI models in the last, like, five years or 10?

Yeah. it's a good question. Yeah. so first, transformers was brought up into the world 10 years ago, nine years ago. so it was a long time before. And even after that, we, we still follow like a similar fundamental framework right now with, with some minor changes like activation layers, mix of expert, mixture of experts that's not always needed, and also some change on how, like local attention, sliding window attentions. But the same, frameworks is still the same as, nine years ago when the paper initially came out. So I think that's the answer to that would be, for me, it would be just the s- the data, the scale of data we train them on, the scale of compute we use to train them. like, like it's, it's, like the, the classic story from GPT-1 to GPT-3, right?

Once you try and train the model, train the basically the same model using more compute, more data, more diverse data, more, internet scale data, we all get this emerging very competitive, performance we, we see now. So I would attribute that to, to, to, to the data and, and also secondarily to the, to the compute, to the how, how, how many, epochs we train on the same data. I think, I think actually, it's mostly data because now we train most models with less or just equal around, around one epoch. Yeah.

astra.text:
Yeah, so I, I would qualify that a little bit. I’m not saying architecture doesn’t matter. I’m saying that once you have a reasonably good architecture, and you explore its design space enough, different choices can get you to a similar level. That’s different from saying you can take any architecture and it will work equally well.

And similarly, with normalization, being able to replace it doesn’t mean that whatever it was doing was unnecessary. You’re replacing it with another operation, right? So the interesting question is, what property do we actually need, and is normalization the only way to get that property? Those are different questions. Sometimes we become very attached to a particular component because it’s in every successful model, but that doesn’t necessarily mean that particular implementation is essential.

So, why do we have much better models now? I think it’s the combination of things. We have more compute, we can train on more data, and we’ve figured out recipes that allow us to actually use that compute and data effectively. Architecture is part of that recipe. A model that doesn’t train well when you make it bigger, or is very inefficient, would prevent you from reaching that point in the first place.

But once you have that foundation, the question becomes, where does the next improvement come from? And that’s where I tend to think more about data. What are we asking the model to learn? What information does it have access to? Can it use the context we give it effectively?

So I don’t think there’s a contradiction. The architectural breakthroughs were very important in getting us here. But that doesn’t imply that changing the architecture is always the most effective way to improve the models we already have. And our work was really trying to understand that distinction, rather than saying architecture never mattered. Yeah.

sol.text:
Yeah, I think I would make a distinction between a specific component and the function that component serves. So normalization itself may not be essential, but stable optimization is essential. Self-attention itself may not be essential, but the ability to communicate information across tokens and to scale efficiently is essential. Residual connections, good signal propagation, sufficient capacity—these more abstract properties matter, even if the exact implementation can change.

And then why only recently? I think it is really the combination of scale, data, compute, and engineering. We found a very simple interface and training objective that can absorb enormous amounts of data, and we developed hardware and systems that let us train these models reliably at very large scale. Transformer was extremely important because it made that scaling convenient and unified different kinds of data, but I would hesitate to say that one architectural operation created intelligence by itself.

So perhaps the core component is actually the learning process: what data the model sees, what objective it learns from, and whether optimization remains stable as you increase the scale. Architecture provides the function approximator and makes that process more or less efficient. Once it is good enough to sit near that Pareto frontier, improvements in the data, context, memory, and compute can matter much more. The recent models are good because all of these pieces matured together, not because we suddenly discovered one indispensable layer. Yeah.

opus.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, that's, that's a great question. So I, I should clarify a bit, when I say architecture doesn't matter that much, I mean it, it matters in a, in a threshold sense, right? Like you need the architecture to not, to not be a bottleneck. You need it to be scalable, you need it to be parallelizable on modern hardware, you need it to be trainable at, at depth, right? So residual connections, normalization or, or some substitute for normalization, these are, these are things that, that unlocked training very deep, very large models. But once you're past that threshold, once you're on the frontier curve, moving along it gives you a few percent, it doesn't give you a new capability. And I think, the, the DyT work, the, the normalization one, it's, it's kind of the same lesson, right? We, we thought normalization layers were doing something very deep and statistical, and, and it turns out a lot of what they do is just, just squashing the extreme values, and you can get that from a, a simple element-wise tanh. So it's again, a lesson about, about our own understanding more than a, a practical must-switch.

So then what actually changed in the last five, ten years? I, I would say three things. one is data, obviously, both the scale and, and more importantly the, the objective that lets you consume it. Like next token prediction on internet-scale text, it's, it's a self-supervised objective that doesn't need labels, so suddenly all of the data is training data. Before that, we were, we were stuck with ImageNet, one million images, thousand classes, and, and you just cannot get very far with that no matter what architecture you use. Second is compute, hardware. and this actually ties back to architecture, because the reason transformers won is, is partly that they map really well onto GPUs, right? It's, it's dense matrix multiplication, it's parallel over the sequence. So it's not that transformer is, is a better inductive bias necessarily, it's that it's a better, better substrate for scaling. And the third is, is honestly just engineering maturity. Like, the, the optimizer, the learning rate schedule, the data cleaning pipelines, the, the infrastructure to train on tens of thousands of chips without it falling over. These are not, not papers people cite, but they are, they're a huge part of why things work now.

And, and more recently I'd add post-training, RL, the, the fact that we learned how to, how to take a pre-trained model and, and actually make it useful and aligned to what people want. So, yeah, if I had to, to rank, it's data and objective first, then compute and, and the systems around it, then architecture. Yeah.

grok.text:
Yeah. Yeah, I, I, I wanna, I wanna slightly push back on, on the framing that architecture is not so important, or that, that normalization is not so important. I, I, I wouldn't quite put it that way.

So, so the, the, the paper you're referring to, yes, that's, that's Dynamic Tanh. The, the observation there is, we, we tend to treat LayerNorm, or BatchNorm, as this, this almost sacred component, right? Like you, you, you cannot train a modern network without it. And, and what we found is, if you replace it with a, a very simple element-wise tanh, with a learnable scale, and you, you treat a few things carefully, the model can still train, and, and can still reach a similar level of performance. So, so the lesson is not that normalization never mattered. The lesson is more like, a lot of things we thought were the, the indispensable core, if you, if you compensate in the right way, they, they can be substituted. It's, it's in the same spirit as ConvNeXt, actually. The, the, the, the identity of the component is less unique than we thought.

So, so then, then what do I think actually matters? I, I would, I would go back to this, this picture of a function approximator. Neural networks are, are how we parameterize a, a very flexible function. And, and there are a few things that, that, that I think are, are genuinely load-bearing.

One is residual connections. Like, this, this idea that you, you keep a path that is close to identity, so that, that depth is usable. Without that, we, we just could not train very deep models stably. Two is some, some mixing mechanism over the input, whether that's convolution, or self-attention, or, or something in between, plus feed-forward layers in the right places, with a reasonable activation. You, you need both a way for information to interact, and a way to transform it nonlinearly. Three is the, the training recipe and the data. Like, what, what distribution are you approximating? How long do you train, at what scale, with what objective? And four, more and more, I think context and memory, how the model can use a long history, how it can keep state, that, that is becoming the, the bottleneck for actually making these systems useful.

So, so why, why only in the last, like, five or ten years, we suddenly have, have these very good models, if, if architecture is, is not this magical missing piece? I, I, I think the, the honest answer is, it was not that we, we finally discovered the one true architecture. Transformers were, were absolutely a breakthrough, I, I said that, especially because they gave us a unified interface over sequences, and then later over images and text together. That, that unification is huge. But, but what really changed is scale, and data, and compute. We, we finally had enough data, enough compute, and a parameterization that was good enough, residual, attention or convolution, feed-forward, norms or something that plays a similar role, that, that the function approximator could actually absorb internet-scale supervision.

If you, if you look at it that way, the last decade is, is less like we invented intelligence in the architecture, and more like we, we finally had a, a trainable enough, scalable enough, general enough function class, and we poured an unprecedented amount of data and compute into it. Architecture still matters in the sense that a bad parameterization will not, will not get you onto that frontier. But once you are on it, the, the next jumps, I, I tend to think, come more from data, from objectives, from context and memory, from how we use these models, than from swapping convolution for attention or, or LayerNorm for tanh. Yeah.

gemini.text:
Yeah, I think the short answer is really scale—both compute and data. 

Like I mentioned earlier, architecture is really just how we parameterize the function approximator. As long as you get a few basic things right—like having residual connections, reasonable mechanisms like self-attention or convolution, and the right activations in the right places—you will already be very close to that Pareto frontier of performance and efficiency. 

What really changed over the last five or ten years isn't necessarily that the architectures became vastly superior, but that we finally have the compute resources to train models at a convincing scale, and massive amounts of data to train them on. And on top of that, we've figured out how to unify data representations—treating vision and text as tokens in a shared framework. 

So from a practical point of view, what has really driven the breakthroughs isn't the subtle architectural tweaks. It's the compute, what data the model is trained on, and how effectively the system can handle scale, context, and memory. Architecture gives you the stable baseline to reach that frontier, but scale and data are what actually push the capabilities forward.

kimi.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I think that's a great question. So, so first, on the, the normalization paper, right, the, the finding there was kind of surprising even to us. Normalization layers have been, for like a decade, been considered this absolutely essential component, right? Like you, you cannot train a deep network without batch norm or layer norm. And what we found is that you can actually replace them with, just a properly scaled, like tanh activation, a, a very cheap element-wise function, and the model trains fine, sometimes even slightly better. So this, this kind of reinforces the lesson from the ConvNeXt work, right? A lot of things we thought were, were fundamental turn out to be, replaceable.

So then what is actually fundamental? I, I would say, there are a few things. One is, of course, gradient-based learning, backpropagation, like the, the whole paradigm of learning from data through, differentiating through a, a big parameterized function. That's, that's the foundation. And then within the architecture, things like residual connections, having some mechanism to mix information across, across tokens or spatial locations, whether it's attention or convolution or something else, and the right nonlinearities. These are, I'd say, the core components. But, but these have existed for a long time, right? Like residual connections are from 2015, even earlier if you, you count some, some prior works. Attention is, is also, several years old now.

So why only now do we have good AI? I, I think the answer is, honestly, scale. Scale of compute and, and scale of data. Like the, the algorithms, the, the core ideas were largely there. What changed is that we, we figured out that if you just train a much bigger model on much more data, with the right training recipe, the, the performance keeps improving in a, in a predictable way. And, and also the hardware caught up. Like the GPUs, the, the infrastructure for distributed training, these are, these are engineering, achievements that, that enabled the science.

And, and the other thing is data, right? Like the internet-scale data. The model is, is essentially a reflection of, of what it has been trained on. The architecture is just the, the container, the, the function approximator. But what's actually inside, the knowledge, the capabilities, comes from the data. So I, I would say if, if you ask me to rank what matters, I'd say data first, then the, the scale, the compute, and then architecture is, is kind of third. As long as you don't make, like, catastrophic mistakes in the architecture, you'll, you'll be close to the frontier.

And, and I think that's also why, going forward, the interesting problems are, are less about, inventing a new building block and more about, how do we, how do we better use data, how do we handle long context and memory, how do we make the model learn continually, right? These, these feel like the, the bottlenecks now, rather than the, the architecture itself. Yeah.

fable.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, so, so first I, I want to clarify a bit. I, I wouldn't say architecture doesn't matter. I, I would say architecture matters, but only up to a point, right? So there is, there is a set of things you need to get right, and, and then once you get them right, the, the remaining choices, like whether you use convolution or self-attention, whether you use LayerNorm or, or something else, they, they don't move you very far from, from the frontier. So the, the normalization paper is, is actually a good example of this. So in that work, we, we looked at what LayerNorm is actually doing inside a trained transformer, and, and we found that the input-output mapping of, of the normalization layer looks like a, like a tanh curve. It's, it's mostly linear in the middle and then it squashes the extreme values. So, so we replaced it with just a tanh of, of alpha times x, with a learnable alpha, and, and it works. But, but I don't read this as, normalization is not important. I read it as, the function normalization was serving is important, and, and it can be served by something much simpler. So, so the, the lesson is more about, what is the actual role of each component, and, and, once you understand the role, you have, more freedom in how you implement it.

So, so if you ask me what are the, the core things, I, I think there are a few. residual connections, I, I think that's, that's the one thing that, is really hard to remove. Like, you need a, a path for gradients and, and for information to, to flow through very deep networks. then you need some, some mechanism for tokens to, to interact with each other, and, and that can be attention, can be convolution, can be, some, some other mixing, and, and you need some, some nonlinearity and, some channel mixing, the feed-forward part. And, and then, there are the things around the network that people, people don't count as architecture, but, but I think they matter a lot. The, the optimizer, the learning rate schedule, the initialization, and, and, having something that controls the, the scale of activations, whether it's normalization or, or a tanh, or, or careful initialization. So, so I, I think of, of, architecture as, as the whole recipe, not just the, the diagram of the blocks.

And, and then to your second question, why, why only now? I, I think it's, it's honestly mostly, compute and data, and, and, the objective. So, so the transformer, I, I think, the biggest gift of the transformer was not that it is more expressive than, than a convnet or, or an RNN. It's, it's that it is very easy to scale on, on the hardware we have. It's, it's very parallel, it maps very well to, to GPUs, and, and it's kind of, uniform, you, you use the same block everywhere, so, so you can, you can build the systems, the infrastructure around it very, very efficiently. And, and then, the, the other thing is that we, we changed what we, train on. So, so before, in, in the vision community, we were, we were training on ImageNet with labels, and, and there is only so much, so much you can learn from, from one million labels.
